_purpose: Established on Menu. Reuse verbatim for Dialog, Tooltip, Snackbar, Popover and any other floating surface.
1_readTheElevation: Find which elevation the component's Paper renders at — read it from source, do not assume. Menu does not set one, so it inherits Popover's `elevation = 8`. Alert uses theme.shadows[3] directly. Autocomplete's paper takes Paper's own default of 1.
2_translateTheShadow: MUI's styles/shadows.js builds every elevation from createShadow(...12 numbers) as THREE stacked CSS layers: umbra px[0..3] at rgba(0,0,0,0.20), penumbra px[4..7] at 0.14, ambient px[8..11] at 0.12. Each group is offsetX, offsetY, blur, spread. Map each to a Figma DROP_SHADOW with offset {x,y}, radius = the CSS blur value, and spread passed through. Never eyeball a drop shadow.
3_makeItAStyle: Create an effect style named 'Elevation / N' carrying all three layers, and apply it with setEffectStyleIdAsync rather than setting node.effects. The style is the binding — it makes the shadow reviewable and changeable in one place, the way variables do for colour.
4_recordProvenance: The Tebra theme passes no `shadows` array, so every elevation is substrate. Say so in the style description and flag it, exactly as with TextField's outline.
5_surfaceAndClipping: Paper gets background.paper, radius shape.borderRadius (4), and clipsContent true to mirror overflow:hidden. Check the list/content padding separately — Tebra's global MuiList disablePadding changes it for List-based surfaces but not for styled-div surfaces.
6_positioning: Read anchorOrigin and transformOrigin from the component source and draw the composition at that offset. Menu: anchor bottom-left to transform top-left, so no gap. Put the composition on background.default, not white, so the elevation is actually legible.
